teaser: The most famous touch in art is a touch that has not happened yet.

lesson.text: Twenty meters. That is roughly how far this scene floats above the chapel floor, about 65 feet, the height of a six-story building. From down there the two fingers at its center are specks. Michelangelo painted them anyway as if the whole world would one day lean in to look. It did.

He had not wanted the job. In 1508 Pope Julius II ordered him to paint the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in Rome. Michelangelo, 33, protested that he was a sculptor, not a painter, and suspected his rivals of setting him up to fail. He signed some letters of those years “Michelangelo, sculptor.”

He did not paint lying on his back. He stood on a scaffold of his own design, head tipped back, arm raised, for four years. In a comic poem to a friend he complained that his beard pointed at heaven and his face was a floor for dripping paint.

The technique is fresco: color brushed onto a patch of fresh, wet plaster, which locks the paint in as it dries. Each patch must be finished in a day. The seams between patches show that this scene took about sixteen such days, Adam's whole body only about four.

The Bible says God shaped the first man from dust and breathed life into his nostrils. Nobody mentions a finger. That is Michelangelo's invention: life passing like a spark across a gap. The two arms that almost meet are built as opposites.
Two arms, two shapes. Compare them one at a time.

lines.label: Adam's arm
lines.text: It is propped on his knee, or it would fall. The wrist bends and the finger droops. All the muscle is there, and none of the will.

lines.label: God's arm
lines.text: Straight as a thrown spear from shoulder to fingertip. The index finger is stretched hard. Everything in this arm is intention.

lines.label: A body that leans back
lines.text: Adam's body is one long hollow curve, sinking into the hillside. He has just been made and has not yet moved.

lines.label: A body that rushes in
lines.text: God's body is the same curve turned the other way and thrown forward. His legs trail behind him and his hair and beard blow back.

lesson.text: The picture's power lies in what is missing. The fingers do not touch, so the moment never ends: you are always one instant before life begins.

Earlier artists had shown God as a stiff, standing ruler, often just a hand in a cloud. Here he flies, barefoot, in a thin pink tunic that shows his knees. He does not travel alone either. A crowd rides with him inside the red cloak, and he holds on to one of them.
God's right hand reaches for Adam. Where is his left hand? Tap it.

spots.title: The other hand
spots.text: His left arm circles a woman's shoulders and his fingers rest on a wide-eyed child. Some scholars see the Christ child here: the plan to save humankind, already in hand as the first human wakes.

lesson.text: So the story does not stop at Adam. Michelangelo packs the future into the cloak. Who the passengers are has never been settled, and the artist left no explanation. That silence has invited some very inventive readings.

In 1990 an American doctor, Frank Meshberger, argued in a medical journal that the cloak and its figures match a cross-section of the human brain. Michelangelo did dissect corpses as a young man to learn anatomy. Whether he hid a brain here cannot be proven.

lesson.title: Three places to stop
lesson.text: With that idea in mind, visit both sides of the gap.

spots.title: Adam's face
spots.text: His eyes are open and fixed on his maker, but the expression is drowsy, almost wistful. He is alive in body. The rest is still on its way.

spots.title: The woman
spots.text: Tucked under God's arm, a young woman stares straight at Adam. Many think she is Eve, waiting to be created. Others say she is Wisdom, God's companion in the Bible.

spots.title: The cloak
spots.text: The red cloth swells around the group like a shell or a sail. Its outline is the shape Meshberger compared to a brain. A womb has been proposed too.

spots.title: The green scarf
spots.text: A ribbon of green streams out below. Its color returns in the hill under Adam, a thin thread tying heaven's side of the picture to earth's.

lesson.text: Michelangelo painted the ceiling from the entrance toward the altar, and after a pause in the work he saw his first scenes from the floor. The figures were too small. Everything he painted afterward, this scene included, is bigger and simpler: two bodies, bare ground, empty sky.
The famous fingertip is not entirely his. A crack opened in the plaster in the 1500s and damaged Adam's hand. A restorer named Domenico Carnevali repainted the ends of the fingers around 1570.

For centuries candle soot and layers of old glue turned the ceiling brown, and people assumed Michelangelo was a gloomy colorist. A cleaning in the 1980s uncovered the pinks, greens and pale sky you see here. Some critics were shocked by how bright it was.

The gap has been borrowed ever since: in cartoons, in advertising, on the poster for the film E.T., where a child's finger meets an alien's. Each copy closes the distance or jokes about it. The original keeps it open, twenty meters up, where it has stayed for five centuries.

quiz.question: How did Michelangelo paint the ceiling?
options: Standing, with his head tipped back
quiz.explanation: He stood on a scaffold he designed and even wrote a poem about the discomfort.

quiz.question: What is fresco?
options: Paint applied to fresh, wet plaster
Oil paint on canvas glued to a wall
quiz.explanation: The drying plaster locks in the color, and each patch must be finished in a day.

quiz.question: How does the Bible say Adam received life?
options: By a touch of God's finger
By God's breath in his nostrils
quiz.explanation: The finger is Michelangelo's own invention.

quiz.question: Where does God's left hand rest?
options: On a child inside the cloak
quiz.explanation: His left arm goes around a woman and his fingers touch a child.

quiz.question: What did Frank Meshberger see in the red cloak?
quiz.explanation: In 1990 he compared its outline to a cross-section of the brain.

quiz.question: Why are the figures in this scene so large and few?
options: The pope asked for fewer figures
He saw that his earlier, smaller figures were hard to read from the floor
quiz.explanation: After a pause he judged the first scenes too small and enlarged everything.

facts.text: The fingers of God and Adam touch.
facts.explanation: A small gap separates them, and that gap is the point of the picture.

facts.text: Michelangelo thought of himself as a sculptor and did not want the commission.
facts.explanation: He protested that painting was not his trade.

facts.text: The ceiling's bright colors were added by restorers in the 1980s.
facts.explanation: The cleaning removed soot and glue and uncovered Michelangelo's own colors.
